name: BURGER A LA MODE - COMES WITH ICE CREAM (Not on top)

recipe.history:
The phrase "à la mode" is a French expression meaning "in the fashion" or "according to the current style," and its culinary roots reach back to seventeenth-century French court cuisine, where it was applied to dishes prepared in the prevailing elegant manner of the day. In France, bœuf à la mode referred specifically to a braised beef pot roast larded with fat, slow-cooked with wine and aromatic vegetables until luxuriously tender — a dish that embodied the haute cuisine ideal of transforming humble ingredients through patient technique into something transcendent. The term migrated freely across the French culinary lexicon, attaching itself to any preparation that was considered fashionable or refined. It was never fixed to ice cream in its homeland; that peculiarly American reassignment came later, a transatlantic reinvention that the French themselves would likely regard with the polite, faintly pained smile they reserve for cultural misunderstandings.

The pairing of ice cream with warm, savory American comfort food is a phenomenon born of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, nurtured in the great democratic kitchens of the Midwest and the lunch counters of the Eastern Seaboard. The most commonly cited origin story places "pie à la mode" at the Cambridge Hotel in upstate New York in the 1890s, when a diner named Charles Watson Townsend allegedly demanded a scoop of vanilla ice cream atop his apple pie and the resulting combination caught the attention of a New York Tribune reporter. Whether apocryphal or not, the story captures something true about the American appetite: the willingness, even the eagerness, to pile one pleasure on top of another. The leap from pie to burger is shorter than it sounds. Both are warm, yielding, richly savory things, and the cold, sweet, fatty creaminess of vanilla ice cream acts on the palate in much the same way — cutting richness, resetting the tongue, offering a counterpoint that makes the next bite of savory food taste more intensely like itself. This is not excess for its own sake; it is, in its unpretentious way, the same logic that drives the great sweet-and-savory pairings of every serious culinary tradition on earth.

I first had something like this burger on a sweltering August afternoon in a small diner outside of Tulsa, the kind of place with a laminated menu held together by optimism and a single strip of scotch tape. The air conditioning was losing its argument with the heat, and the ceiling fan moved the warm air around in slow, unconvincing circles. I ordered a cheeseburger because there was nothing else I wanted, and the waitress — without being asked, without ceremony — set a small bowl of vanilla ice cream on the tray beside the plate. "Goes with it," she said, as if this were a law of nature I had simply failed to encounter yet. She was right. The cold cream against the warm, yielding beef, the sweetness against the char and the salt, the way both things became more themselves in contrast — I ate slowly, the way you eat when you realize you are in the presence of something that will become a memory. That diner is probably gone now. The feeling is not.

There is one correct internal temperature for a beef patty, and it is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius, achieved over high dry heat and rested briefly before it meets the bun. This is not a matter of preference in the way that, say, mustard versus mayo is a matter of preference. It is a matter of what beef actually is and what heat actually does to it. Below that range the fat has not fully rendered, the Maillard crust has not developed its full architectural complexity, and the texture is slack and unresolved. Above it — and this is where so many well-meaning burgers go to die — the myosin proteins have seized, the moisture has fled, and what remains is a disc of meat that is, at best, merely fine. At medium rare the fat is liquid and present, the juices are contained within a crust that has genuine color and bitterness to balance the richness, and the center is soft, yielding, and deeply red in a way that communicates life and care. Cook it further if you must, but understand that you are making a different dish, and a lesser one. This burger, served beside its small cold scoop of vanilla, deserves the respect of being cooked correctly.
ingredients: 300g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
680g (1.5 lbs) freshly ground beef blend: 60% chuck (80/20), 40% short rib
Neutral oil (such as canola) for the griddle or cast iron
120ml neutral oil (canola or light olive oil)
4 slices American cheese (or mild cheddar, for melting)
1 medium white onion, thinly sliced into rings
1 large beefsteak tomato, sliced into 1/4-inch rounds
1 head butter lettuce, leaves separated and washed
Kosher dill pickles, sliced into coins
FOR THE VANILLA ICE CREAM (served on the side, NOT on top):
1 whole vanilla bean, split and scraped
instructions: 1. MAKE THE ICE CREAM BASE (do this first — needs overnight freezing). Combine the heavy cream, whole milk, half the sugar (75g), vanilla bean pod, and scraped seeds in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Warm until steaming and just beginning to simmer at the edges; do not boil. Remove from heat.
2. In a large bowl, whisk the egg yolks with the remaining 75g sugar and the pinch of salt until the mixture is pale yellow and slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.
3. Temper the hot cream into the yolks: while whisking constantly, slowly ladle about half the hot cream mixture into the yolks in a thin stream. Pour the tempered mixture back into the saucepan.

4. Cook the custard over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula and scraping the bottom of the pan, until it thickens enough to coat the back of the spatula and reads 77–80°C (170–175°F) on an instant-read thermometer. Do not boil.

5. Strain the custard through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl set over an ice bath. Discard the vanilla pod. Stir in the vanilla extract. Cool the custard to room temperature, stirring occasionally, then cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight.

6. Churn the chilled custard in an ice cream maker according to the manufacturer's instructions until thick and creamy, about 20–25 minutes. Transfer to a freezer-safe container and freeze for at least 4 hours until firm.

7. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS. In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook, combine the bread flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt. Mix briefly to combine. Add 2 eggs and the warm milk. Mix on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.

8. Increase speed to medium and knead for 5 minutes until the dough comes together. With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter a few cubes at a time, waiting for each addition to be fully incorporated before adding the next. This will take about 8–10 minutes total. The dough should be smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky.
9. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, about 1.5 to 2 hours.

10. Punch down the dough and divide it into 4 equal portions (about 130g each). Shape each into a tight, smooth ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching the seam underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them at least 3 inches apart.
11. Cover loosely with oiled plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature for 45–60 minutes, until noticeably puffed.
12. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water to make an egg wash. Brush the tops of the buns gently and evenly. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using.
13. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

14. MAKE THE HOMEMADE MAYONNAISE. In a small bowl, whisk together the egg yolk, Dijon mustard, and lemon juice. While whisking vigorously, add the oil in an extremely slow, thin, steady stream — drop by drop at first — until the mixture begins to emulsify and thicken. Once about a third of the oil is incorporated and the emulsion is stable, you can add the remaining oil in a slightly faster thin stream. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

15. MAKE THE SPECIAL SAUCE. Combine the mayonnaise, ketchup, yellow mustard, relish, apple cider vinegar, smoked paprika, onion powder, and cayenne in a bowl. Whisk until smooth and uniform. Taste and adjust seasoning. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to allow flavors to meld.

16. PREPARE THE PATTIES. Remove the ground beef blend from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Gently divide the meat into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Handle the meat as little as possible. Form each portion loosely into a ball, then press into a patty about 3/4 inch thick. Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty — this prevents it from doming as it cooks. Season both sides generously with kosher salt, black pepper, and garlic powder immediately before cooking.

17. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE. Heat a cast iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place the patties in the pan without crowding — cook in batches if needed. Do not press the patties. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms on the bottom.

18. Flip each patty once. Immediately place a slice of cheese on top of each patty. Cook for 2 more minutes. Check the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer: target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove from heat at 128°F (53°C) as carryover cooking will bring it to temperature during rest.
19. Transfer patties to a clean plate and tent loosely with foil. Rest for 3–4 minutes. Do not skip the rest. The juices must redistribute.

20. TOAST THE BUNS. While the patties rest, split the brioche buns and place cut-side down in the same pan over medium heat (add a small amount of butter if desired). Toast for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped.

21. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER. Spread a generous layer of special sauce on both the top and bottom bun cut faces. On the bottom bun, layer: butter lettuce leaves, 2 slices of tomato, the rested cheeseburger patty, a few rings of raw white onion, and dill pickle coins. Cap with the top bun.

22. PLATE AND SERVE. Place the assembled burger on a plate or in a paper-lined basket. To the side — not on top, as the name explicitly and correctly demands — place a small scoop (approximately 60–75g) of the vanilla ice cream in a chilled ramekin or small bowl. Serve immediately while the burger is hot and the ice cream is still cold and firm. The contrast is the point.
